summary: Specifies which cryptographic algorithms implementations of IPsec ESP and AH must or should support, to ensure interoperability among different products. It was replaced by RFC 7321.

plainLanguage.summary: So that different companies' IPsec products can talk, this lists which scramblers and signers every product must know. It was later replaced.

subtitle: Specify which encryption and authentication algorithms every IPsec product must support to ensure interoperability.

tldr.problem: IPsec implementations from different vendors use different cryptographic algorithms, so two products may not be able to communicate if they have no algorithms in common.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines which algorithms each IPsec implementation must, should, or may support. It lists mandatory-to-implement algorithms (AES-CBC encryption and HMAC-SHA1 authentication) that all implementations must have, plus optional algorithms that may be used if both sides support them.
tldr.outcome: By requiring all IPsec products to implement a common baseline of algorithms, interoperability is guaranteed: any two IPsec implementations can negotiate a secure connection. The document also identifies algorithms likely to become mandatory in the future, encouraging early adoption.

today: RFC 4835 was obsoleted by RFC 7321 in January 2014. Both documents define mandatory algorithm implementation for ESP and AH, but RFC 7321 updated the requirements based on cryptographic developments and evolved usage.

sections.title: Why Standards for Algorithms
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH) are the two main IPsec mechanisms for protecting data. Both rely on cryptographic algorithms for encryption (ESP) and authentication (both). Different implementations might choose different algorithms based on performance, preference, or availability. Without a common baseline, two products might negotiate a connection but find they have no algorithms in common.

This RFC solves that problem by specifying which algorithms are mandatory-to-implement, which are recommended, and which may be used if both sides support them. The mandatory algorithms change over time as cryptographic attacks improve and new algorithms mature, so this document is separate from the main IPsec specifications and can be updated independently.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine everyone has a different secret code. You need to agree on a code before you can send secret messages. This document says everyone must know at least one code so any two people can talk in secret.

sections.title: ESP and AH Algorithms
sections.content:
ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) can provide encryption, authentication, or both. When encryption is used, it must protect the payload data. Authentication, when used, protects the entire ESP packet. The RFC divides ESP algorithms into two categories: traditional encryption and authentication pairs, and combined mode algorithms that provide both services in one step (such as AES-GCM).

AH (Authentication Header) provides only authentication; it verifies the integrity and authenticity of packets but does not encrypt them. The AH algorithms listed in this RFC are authentication algorithms only, not encryption.

For both ESP and AH, implementations negotiate which algorithm to use through the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol or through pre-configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: ESP is like a locked box that hides your message (encryption) and signs it (authentication). AH is just a signature that proves the message is real and was not changed.

sections.title: Mandatory and Recommended Algorithms
sections.content:
For ESP encryption, all implementations MUST support NULL (no encryption) and AES-CBC with 128-bit keys. TripleDES-CBC is MUST- (still required but expected to be phased out). AES-CTR is SHOULD+ (recommended and likely to become mandatory). DES is SHOULD NOT (deprecated and not recommended).

For ESP authentication, all implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA1-96. AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is SHOULD+ (recommended). HMAC-MD5-96 and NULL are optional.

For AH, the same authentication algorithms apply: HMAC-SHA1-96 is MUST, AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is SHOULD+, and HMAC-MD5-96 is optional.

Combined mode algorithms like AES-CCM and AES-GCM are noted as algorithms of interest and adopted in standards like 802.11i (wireless) and 802.1ae (Ethernet security), though no combined mode algorithm is yet mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IPsec product must know how to do AES encryption and HMAC-SHA1 signing. Some must also know TripleDES. Some should know AES-XCBC. Some optional ones are older or weaker.

sections.title: Cryptographic Strength and Evolution
sections.content:
The strength of a cryptosystem depends on both the algorithm and the key. The algorithms identified as MUST or SHOULD in this RFC are not known to be broken and are believed to remain secure into the foreseeable future. However, cryptographic research is ongoing, and algorithms once considered strong can later be found weak.

This is why the mandatory algorithms are conservative choices: AES was selected because it is widely adopted, thoroughly analyzed, and resistant to known attacks. SHA-1 has weaknesses in collision resistance, but its use in HMAC-SHA1 is not affected by these weaknesses. As new attacks emerge or new algorithms mature, the RFC will be updated to reflect current best practices.
sections.plainLanguage: We picked strong scramblers that many experts have studied hard. If we find a better one later, we can change the rules.

items.label: AES-CBC (128-bit)
items.desc: Advanced Encryption Standard in CBC mode; modern and widely used.

items.label: TripleDES-CBC
items.desc: Three rounds of DES; still required but expected to be phased out.

items.label: AES-CTR
items.desc: AES in counter mode; efficient and likely to become mandatory.

items.label: DES-CBC
items.desc: Single DES; small key size and broken, not recommended.
